content: 1. The prevalence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) among survey age groups born after the introduction of universal hepatitis B vaccination should be reported. This includes the sample size, point prevalence percentage, and the 95% confidence interval. It is essential to ensure that the HBsAg point prevalence for children aged 5 years is included, if available. 2. The data can be extended to provide national and regional estimates, if such information is available. 3. Any findings related to specific subpopulations should be commented on in detail. 4. Study limitations should be clearly outlined, including any constraints in data collection, analysis, or interpretation. 5. The funding source for the hepatitis B vaccination program should be specified. This includes whether the program is self-funded by the country, supported by Gavi (the Vaccine Alliance), or funded by other sources, which should be explicitly mentioned. 6. Plans to sustain or improve hepatitis B immunization coverage should be described. This may include strategies to maintain high coverage rates, address gaps, or enhance program efficiency. 7. Immunization coverage data for hepatitis B (HepB3) over the last five years should be reviewed. This includes whether the coverage has been consistently below 90%, between 90% and 95%, or above 95%. 8. District-level HepB3 coverage should also be assessed. This includes whether coverage is below 80%, above 80%, or above 90% in all districts. 9. The dropout rate between the first dose (HepB1) and the third dose (HepB3) should be analyzed. This includes whether the dropout rate is greater than 5%, less than 5%, or less than 3%. 10. The quality of coverage data should be evaluated. This includes whether only administrative data is available, whether both administrative and survey data are available but inconsistent, or whether both data sources are available and consistent. 11. Serological surveys should be conducted to assess hepatitis B coverage. The timing of these surveys relative to achieving acceptable coverage levels should be noted, such as whether the survey was conducted before or after five years of acceptable coverage. 12. Relevant age groups targeted in the survey should be specified. This includes children under 5 years of age, children aged 5 years or older born during the national vaccination period, or multiple cohorts of children aged 5 years or older born during the vaccination period. 13. Convenience samples are generally not acceptable for verification purposes. However, if a country can provide strong evidence that the sample is representative, these data may be considered. 14. Sustainability of the hepatitis B vaccination program should be assessed. This includes whether there are no plans for sustainability, whether the program is sustainable based on implementation over the past five years, or whether plans are in place to sustain or improve the program to achieve the goal of reducing HBsAg prevalence to ≤1%. 15. The vaccination program's funding mechanism should be described, including whether it is self-funded with a national budget line item, integrated into a national plan, or specified in a comprehensive multi-year plan (cMYP). The cMYP should include specific targets for hepatitis B control through immunization and be cross-linked with the national hepatitis B control strategy. 16. The World Health Organization (WHO) Expert Panel for hepatitis B verification has specific terms of reference. These include conducting desk reviews of country-submitted data, visiting countries and WHO offices as required, participating in technical meetings, and making recommendations to the Regional Director regarding the achievement of the target to reduce HBsAg prevalence to <1% among children over 5 years old. 17. Members of the Verification Expert Panel (VEP) must complete a WHO declaration of interest form and confidentiality agreement. They serve in their personal capacity and do not represent the interests of any specific group or stakeholder. 18. All documents, presentations, and reports presented to the VEP are confidential and may not be disclosed or used without prior approval. VEP members cannot speak or act on behalf of WHO without prior consent. 19. VEP members are not remunerated for their participation but will have travel expenses covered by WHO in accordance with its policies. 20. Operational procedures for the VEP include regular interaction with the secretariat and chairperson, in-person or teleconference meetings as needed, and the circulation of agendas and relevant documents in advance. 21. A summary report of VEP meetings will be circulated for comments and endorsement within two weeks of the meeting. Members are required to respond within two weeks of receiving the communication. 22. When review teams complete the desk data review for verification of the regional hepatitis B control goal, the VEP will discuss and approve the report submitted by the review team either at a meeting or through other means of communication. 23. For conflict of interest reasons, VEP members will not participate in the review team for their own country. 24. The verification process for achieving the regional target for hepatitis B control through immunization involves several steps. First, the Ministry of Health submits data and information to WHO, including a request to initiate the process. Second, WHO convenes a verification team of three independent experts. Third, the verification team reviews the data, liaises with the Ministry of Health for additional information if needed, and informs WHO of its recommendations. 25. The verification process is essential to document the achievement of the target and to strengthen public health programs. Countries are encouraged to initiate the process and provide the necessary data and information. 26. WHO will provide further instructions and assistance through designated focal points or contact persons.
